doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Scobey, Clancy Hayes and Earl Hines as bandleaders
summary: He describes Scobey and Hayes, then Hines's easy leadership and open mind, including his bebop-filled band.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Well of all the people you’ve played with over the years, is there one that stands out as a terrifically interesting character?

Well Scobey was a very fine trumpet player. He loved Louis and Scobey of course had played classical music as well as jazz so his musicianship — he had excellent musicianship. He and Clancy Hayes. Clancy Hayes, oh man I think he was from Parsons, Kansas and so he knew all the Mississippi River lore. The first time I heard Scott Joplin’s name it was from Clancy Hayes. Jack Brook, excellent trombonist, excellent musician. My Dixieland experience, they were good musicians and kind of like characters. Fatha Hines, now he was a legend, and I just couldn’t believe it when I looked up and I’m on the same bandstand with him. And he was easy to work for because he just wanted you to © Fillius Jazz Archive -32-

do your thing, play your part. And he would size you up and see what you could do, so I had an extended solo with the band. As a matter of fact I’ve got a record out, oh what the heck I’ve even forgotten what the name of it is.
Is it the Monday Night thing?

Yeah. I’ve got an extended solo on that. And so he was very interesting and he was a fantastic musician. Keys didn’t mean anything, play in any key. He had a style. Now he wasn’t really a bebopper but there was, at one time, one of his bands was loaded with beboppers. He had Bird, he had Diz, he had J.J. Johnson, he had all the beboppers in his band at one time. And they claim that was during the record ban, when they couldn’t do any recordings.
